## base R plotting in 1961: <br> The ZUSE plotter Z64

![](https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Liss-Werner/publication/328760933/figure/fig2/AS:689916614832132@1541500347361/Automatisches-Zeichengeraet-ZUSE-Z64-flatbed-drawing-machine-Graphomat-Z64-photograph-by.png)

# 1. Principal Component Regression (PCR)

```{r echo=FALSE, cache=FALSE}
library(scran)
library(scater)
library(patchwork)
```

- has been used to evaluate batch correction.
- e.g., Almut's `CellMixS` cites `kBet`,    
  and both use PCR as an evaluation metric.
- however, the variability attributable to  
  batch is aggregated across, say, 100 PCs.

# Let's instead...

1. do PCR against clusters.
2. what can we learn from the PCs?

## A real-life example

Mereu et al. (2020) benchmark of 13 scRNA-seq platforms

![R2 from PCR against batch & cluster, <br> before & after integration](Mereu20.png)

## Getting set up {.smaller}

```{r fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
#| layout-ncol: 2
(sce <- readRDS("pbmc4k.rds"))
plotTSNE(sce, colour_by="Louvain")
```

## Closer look at PCs {.smaller}

PC1 is essentially a contrast between two subsets of clusters.

```{r fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
ids <- sce$Louvain
pcs <- reducedDim(sce, "PCA")
boxplot(pcs[, 1] ~ ids)
abline(h=0, col="red")
```

## PC Regression {.smaller}

```{r}
fit <- lm(pcs ~ ids)
summary(fit)[[1]]
```

## Multiple R-squared across PCs {.smaller}

- here: proportion of the variation in each PC  
  that can be explained by cluster assignments

```{r fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
pv <- attr(pcs, "percentVar")
r2 <- sapply(summary(fit), \(.) .$adj.r.squared)
plot(pv/max(pv), type="b", xlab="PC", 
  ylab = "PV (black) / R2 (red)")
lines(r2, type="b", col="red")
```

## Closer look at PC4 {.smaller}

What is that set of PC4-high cells?

:::: {layout-ncol=2}

::: {.column}

```{r fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
plot(pcs[, c(4, 1)], col=ids, asp=1)
abline(v=0, h=0)
```

:::

::: {.column}

```{r fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
ns <- table(ids[pcs[, 4] > 10])
(k <- names(which.max(ns)))
es <- logcounts(sce)[, ids == k]
head(sort(rowSds(es, useNames=TRUE), dec=TRUE), 5)
```
Some of these are platelet factors.  
The first is a sign of platelet activation.

:::

::::

```{r fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
gs <- c("PPBP", "PF4", "GNG11", "HIST1H2AC")
plotExpression(sce, gs, "Louvain", color_by="Louvain")
```

## Another example {.smaller}

- no correlation with size factors or zero-fraction

```{r eval=FALSE}
cor(pcs[, 6], sce$sizeFactor) # 0.053
cor(pcs[, 6], colMeans(counts(sce) == 0)) # -0.076
```

- nothing apparent going on with clusters either

```{r fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
#| layout-ncol: 1
plot(pcs[, c(1, 6)], col=ids, asp=1)
```

## Rotation

- rotations = loadings on each of the genes for each PC
- which genes drive PC6?

```{r}
rot <- attr(pcs, "rotation")
head(sort(abs(rot[, 6]), dec=TRUE))
```

## What does ChatGPT thing? {.smaller}

Do the genes FOS and DUSP1 interact and if so, how?

- FOS interacts with JUN and JUNB to form the AP-1 transcription factor complex,  
which activates DUSP1 and other genes in the list.

- FOS is an immediate early gene that encodes a transcription factor known as c-Fos.  
It is typically induced rapidly in response to various extracellular stimuli,  
such as growth factors, hormones, and stress signals.

Google search: 10.1007/s10911-020-09448-1

> Here, we show that the AP-1 transcription factor components,  
i.e., JUN, JUNB, FOS, FOSB, in addition to DUSP1, EGR1, NR4A1,  
IER2 and BTG2, behave as a conserved co-regulated group of  
genes whose expression is associated to ZFP36 in cancer cells.

## 2. Isolation Random Forests

- interpretable, easy to run, not too slow.
- perhaps something useful for outlier detection?

```{r}
# let's make up a cell...
ol <- runif(ncol(pcs), -20, 20)
qcs <- rbind(pcs, ol)

# ...and find it
library(isotree)
irf <- isolation.forest(qcs, ndim=NULL, ntrees=100)
iso <- predict(irf, qcs)
summary(iso)
```

***

```{r fig.width=6, fig.height=6}
#| layout-ncol: 1
# let's see if we got it:
pal <- rev(hcl.colors(n <- 100, "Reds"))
plot(qcs, asp=1, lwd=2, cex=iso, col=pal[cut(iso, n)])
```
